    #122697. 11 Warm-Weather Destinations to Flock to This Winter

    📅 26 Sep 2025 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2653 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    11 Warm-Weather Destinations to Flock to This Winter

    📅 26 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2653 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that arguably the best way to overcome winter is to pretend like it’s not happening—i.e., jetting off to a warm-weather destination, where seasons are not taken very seriously and an outdoor adventure is always on the table.
    • Whether you’re interested in hiking to the wild and wondrous waterfalls of Puerto Rico’s El Yunque National Rainforest, snorkeling through the kaleidoscopic waters of Belize’s barrier reef, or simply want to kick back and relax with a dip in Costa Rica’s hot springs, these sunny locations are bound to cure those cold-weather blues.
    • When to go: JanuaryAverage winter temperature: 80–85 degrees.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that arguably the best way to overcome winter is to pretend like it’s not happening—i.e., jetting off to a warm-weather destination, where seasons are not taken very seriously and an outdoor adventure is always on the table. The best winter vacation destinations offer comfortable temperatures, off-peak advantages, and festive happenings. On this list, you’ll find some of the usual suspects, from Punta Cana to the US Virgin Islands, as well as locales you might not have considered (far too often, travelers forget vibrant Marrakech is a shorter-haul Mediterranean option).

    Whether you’re interested in hiking to the wild and wondrous waterfalls of Puerto Rico’s El Yunque National Rainforest, snorkeling through the kaleidoscopic waters of Belize’s barrier reef, or simply want to kick back and relax with a dip in Costa Rica’s hot springs, these sunny locations are bound to cure those cold-weather blues. So, trade your snow boots for flip-flops and get to plotting your next escape.

    When to go: JanuaryAverage winter temperature: 80–85 degrees.

    According to recent reports, if you’ve been looking for an excuse to finally book that trip to Hawaii, shoot for after the holiday rush, when flights get significantly cheaper. January might be the start of rainy season in Maui, but the showers are often short and localized; for the most part, you’ll enjoy sunshiny days with temperatures that hover in the low-80s. Humpback whales make their way from Alaska around this time, and you can spot the giant beauties from Papawai Point on Honoapiilani Highway, an overlook facing the ʻAuʻau Channel. If you’re not afraid of big waves, heavy north swells at this time of year make for excellent surfing, especially at Ho‘okipa Beach Park. The Road to Hana, a scenic and beautiful drive at any time of year, becomes especially lush in the winter after the rain has fallen, and you’ll likely avoid the crowds too. Along the way, hit up sites like the Twin Falls or the black sand beach at Waianapanapa State Park.

    Where to stay: A Condé Nast Traveler Triple Crown winner, Hāna-Maui Resort, a luxurious off-grid escape, is the pot of gold at the end of the Road to Hana, while Hotel Wailea offers an adults-only vibe on the southwestern coast. Though much humbler, Jimi Hendrix’s former gingerbread-style home, now available for rent on Airbnb, is also a fair contender for your home away from home, surrounded by all kinds of fruit trees and perfectly positioned for daily rainbows.

    When to go: December–JanuaryAverage winter temperature: 65 degrees.

    While you won’t be breaking a sweat in San Diego come December, it’s an excellent place to escape to around the holidays for festive fun in mild, mid-60-degree temperatures. The Parade of Lights is a classic seasonal event, when over 100 private boats get decked out in twinkling lights and sail around San Diego Bay (watch from spots like Shelter Island or Seaport Village on select nights in December). Between November and January, you can also enjoy ice skating without the chill at the Hotel del Coronado, where you’ll glide alongside the Pacific. They say San Diego sunsets are best in the winter, when the sun cuts a path closer to the horizon and there’s not as much coastal marine fog—one of the best places to catch one is Sunset Cliffs Natural Park on the Point Loma peninsula.

    Where to stay: La Valencia, otherwise known as the “Pink Lady” of La Jolla, is one of San Diego’s most iconic stays, and you might hear a seal or two barking in the distance. For unparalleled mountain views, consider this glass house overlooking Sweetwater Regional Park.

    When to go: December–MarchAverage winter temperature: 70–85 degrees.

    According to recent reports, for a Caribbean escape with outdoor adventure, cultural festivals, and farm-to-table splendor, head to Puerto Rico. From December to March, you can take advantage of the dry season on the island, which means your days won’t be interrupted by sudden showers. Holiday festivities continue well beyond Christmas, from Three Kings Day on January 6—the oldest of these celebrations takes place in Juana Díaz, with a reenactment of the Magi on horseback—to the San Sebastian Street Festival, when the namesake street in Old San Juan is filled with art vendors, live music, and plenty of mofongo (January 21–24 this year). Winter is also a great time to explore El Yunque National Forest when it’s not shrouded in unbearable humidity—hike to La Coca Waterfall, take in the green canopy from Yokahú Tower, and keep an ear out for singing coquí frogs.

    Where to stay: For luxe accommodations just a 25-minute drive from El Yunque, look no further than Four Seasons Resort and Residences Puerto Rico, which coordinates guided treks with a strong emphasis on Indigenous history. Condado Ocean Club offers direct access to the beach, while this lakefront retreat near Cueva Ventana and Arecibo Observatory is ideal for couples seeking verdant views.

    When to go: December–MarchAverage winter temperature: 85 degrees.

    Sources indicate that another destination where US travelers can leave their passports at home, the US Virgin Islands are a quintessential Caribbean paradise. December through March is peak season, and there are plenty of reasons why—no rain, calm seas, and temperatures that hover between 77 and 85 degrees, to name a few. St. Croix, the largest of the USVI’s three main islands, is defined by the white sands of Rainbow Beach, as well as its Danish ancestry, which you can explore at colonial-era sites like Fort Frederik and Fort Christiansvaern. St. John is filled with all kinds of natural wonders; take the Underwater Snorkel Trail at Trunk Bay to peer at parrotfish, or set off on the three-mile Reef Bay Trail to hike among pre-Columbian petroglyphs painted by Taíno Indians. St. Thomas is a bustling port with cosmopolitan charm, and you’d be well advised to sample a few conch fritters at Gladys' Café. Whichever island you choose, clear skies and turquoise waters await.

    Industry observers note that where to stay: One of Traveler’s favorite private island resorts (and the only one in the US Virgin Islands), Lovango Resort and Beach Club is located across St. John’s Caneel Bay and offers all kinds of eco-chic accommodations, from wooden treehouses to explorer-style tents. The Westin St. Thomas is set right in front of the harbor, with a stellar spa worth traveling for. For something a bit more intimate, this light-filled, two-bedroom cottage is just a five-minute walk away from Cruz Beach.

    When to go: December–FebruaryAverage winter temperature: 65 degrees.

    While temperatures do drop in Marrakech during the winter—the peaks of the Atlas Mountains will be blanketed in snow—you’ll see far more sun than in certain parts of the US; plus, it’s all the more reason to enjoy a steamy hammam. Winter is a great time to explore the city's popular sites with thinner crowds: comb through the medina’s bustling souks for fragrant spices and a pair of babouche slippers, take in the cobalt blue buildings at the Jardin Majorelle, or learn about one of France’s most legendary fashion designers at the Yves Saint Laurent Museum. Keep an eye out for the dates of the Marrakech International Film Festival, which takes place between the months of November and December—this year it falls from November 20 to 28, and features 76 films from 39 countries.

    Where to stay: Traveler contributor Jordan Lippe-McGraw is a substantial fan of this family-friendly villa, with a heated pool, hammam, and cinema room. A Triple Crown winner, La Mamounia is the city’s grand dame. As global features director Erin Florio puts it, “Every inch of this palatial property has been hyper-considered to make the guest feel as though they have arrived in some regal estate of an Arabian kingdom.” At the Royal Mansour, all riads come with 24/7 access to a private butler.

    When to go: December–AprilAverage winter temperature: 80–90 degrees.

    The Arenal Volcano looms over Costa Rica’s La Fortuna region, heating its natural springs, and there’s a greater chance you’ll see it without cloud cover in the winter. For travelers seeking a combo of adventure and relaxation, La Fortuna (about a three-hour drive from San José) is well-suited for both. Hike through cooled lava fields at Arenal Volcano National Park or swim around La Fortuna Waterfall, then take advantage of nature’s healing powers at Tabacón Thermal Resort and Spa. For a truly memorable experience, book a tour with Arenal Horse Tours and ride your steed straight into the Arenal River for a refreshing dip.

    It has been revealed that where to stay: While Tabacón is perhaps the most iconic resort in the area, The Springs Resort & Spa is another great option, boasting two dozen hot springs, pools, and waterfalls spread across the 65-acre property. If you’re looking for something more intimate, this forest cabin features a private spring-fed pool, rain shower, and marked hiking trails—a one-of-a-kind off-grid retreat.

    When to go: December–AprilAverage winter temperature: 80–85 degrees.

    In a recent development, though small, this Central American country offers a diversity of experiences, whether you want to take it slow in a charming fishing village or ascend new heights in the jungle. Perhaps the most popular destination on Belize’s tourism map, Ambergris Caye is a departure point for the country’s barrier reef—though just south of Ambergris Caye, Caye Caulker provides a nice alternative. While on the car-free island, book a tour with Ragga Sail Adventures for a half-day snorkel through Hol Chan Marine Reserve, the oldest marine reserve in the country. Further south in Punta Gorda, you’ll find rugged adventures and a strong sense of Mayan culture. Here, you’ll have access to several offshore cayes (Belize has hundreds of these small islands, brimming with marine life), from Snake Cayes to Sapodilla Cayes Marine Reserve; if you prefer jungle, take a boat tour through the Monkey River, or hike to the waterfall at Rio Blanco National Park. And be sure to explore the surrounding Toledo District for Mayan ruins, like the Lubaantun, which dates back to 700–900 AD and is also an excellent site for birdwatching.

    Sources indicate that where to stay: Nestled within the Belizean rainforest, Copal Tree Lodge’s jungle suites will make you feel as though you’re suspended among the trees. Wake up to the sounds of monkeys every morning, then take a farm tour around the surrounding property, where you’ll discover how cacao, vanilla, and sugar cane grow. Over in San Pedro, Alaia Belize is your luxury option, just 600 yards away from the barrier reef, while this tiny home will make you feel as though you’re vacationing in a fairy tale.

    When to go: December–AprilAverage winter temperature: 80 degrees.

    According to recent reports, december through April is peak vacation time in Punta Cana, when the rainy season has subsided and there’s not a cloud in the sky. With average highs in the 80s and average lows in the 70s, you’re likely to experience perfect weather during your stay. Come February, you’ve got a good chance of spotting some humpback whales if you cast your eyes off the coast of the Península de Samaná, where they typically pass through until April. The country also celebrates Independence Day in February—on the 27th, to be exact. Visit around that time, and you’re bound to run into a Carnaval parade or bachata dance circle. With the Cordillera Oriental mountain range looming in the background and a selection of cenotes around town—from Hoyo Azul to Hoyo Claro—mountain buggy excursions and diving adventures await even in the winter.

    Recent findings suggest that where to stay: The W Punta Cana redefines the all-inclusive resort as we know it with top-tier dining and some of the largest rooms in the country. Hyatt Vivid Punta Cana, which just opened its doors in August 2026, is another upscale all-inclusive in the area, boasting swim-out suites and a chic speakeasy. If you’ve got kids in tow but still want to experience the height of luxury, Eden Roc Cap Cana is a consistent Readers' Choice Awards winner. For a villa the whole family will enjoy, this eight-bedroom Airbnb in Tortuga Bay comes with a private pool.

    When to go: December–AprilAverage winter temperature: 70 degrees.

    Another prime location for whale watching, Baja California’s southern tip sees the migration of humpback and gray whales between the months of December and April (you might even elect to swim with whale sharks, too, which roam around the nearby Bay of La Paz around this time). You’ll have just missed the rainy season in November, making way for sunny, 70-degree beach days and not-too-chilly evenings. The creative town of Todos Santos boasts a number of art galleries to pop into, like Galeria de Todos Santos and La Sonrisa de la Muerte, while the Sierra de la Laguna mountains are home to stunning trails and swimming holes. If you’re a surfer, Playa Los Cerritos and Playa San Pedro offer some of Mexico’s best waves.

    Industry observers note that where to stay: Todos Santos is home to a number of cutting-edge boutique hotels. Hotel San Cristobal, with its vibrant interiors and delectably fresh seafood, perfectly embodies the bohemian vibes of this tiny surf town. Paradero Todos Santos, located on a five-and-a-half-acre farm, is designed around outdoor adventure: Pick the “Unbound” option, and surfing, hiking, and biking experiences will all be included in the nightly fare. If you prefer to go the rental route, this little bungalow is set among farmland in Pescadero, with its own private rooftop.

    When to go: December–FebruaryAverage winter temperature: 75 degrees.

    Miami is a good idea any time of year, but December through February is considered the dry season, promising temperatures in the mid-70s. Two key events pop up this time of year: Art Basel Miami, in December (4–6, this year), and the South Beach Wine & Food Festival, in February (running the 25–28 in 2027). But there’s always something to do in the Magic City, whether that’s taking a peek into the Pérez Art Museum, spending money in the Design District, or having a stroll through the Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden.

    Where to stay: To embrace the happy-go-lucky spirit of the locals, check in to the Goodtime Hotel and sip on a Purple Reign cocktail (co-owner Pharrell’s favorite drink) at the rooftop pool club. If you’d like to tap into the city’s Art Deco architectural history, stay at The Moore, where you’ll be close to Wynwood and Downtown Miami. This dreamy loft in Collins Park, just a short walk to the beach, is a good bet too.

    When to go: December–FebruaryAverage winter temperature: 85 degrees.

    In a recent development, depending on where you’re coming from, Cape Town might be a little out of the way. But the US's winter is their summer, and with that comes sunny days and a dry, Mediterranean-like climate. Around mid-January, tourists start to flee and kids return to school, making popular attractions more accessible. Take a cable car (or hike, if you’re feeling bold) up to the famous Table Mountain, or drive to Boulders Beach, which boasts one of the last colonies of African penguins in the world. There are plenty of opportunities to engage with some art, as well, from the contemporary galleries at Zeitz MOCAA to the rainbow houses of the Bo-Kaap Museum. And if you’re feeling especially adventurous, you can treat Cape Town as a jumping-off point for the famed Garden Route road trip.

    Recent findings suggest that where to stay: For views of both Table Mountain and the V&A Waterfront, stay at the Silo Hotel, housed in a former grain silo and famous for its maximalist interior design. For something a little more off-the-beaten-path, Ellerman House is an Edwardian mansion turned boutique hotel situated in the exclusive Bantry Bay area. And if it's privacy you're after, this three-bedroom bungalow in St. James features a private hot tub and covered deck with gorgeous sea views.

    #122696. Why International First Class Has Failed At US Airlines (But Shouldn’t)

    In a recent development, we’ve just seen American formally retire its Boeing 777 first class, and with that, no airline in the United States has a “true” international first class anymore. It’s the end of an era, because going back many decades, premium products were largely pioneered by US carriers. So I think this raises the question — why can US carriers not make first class work in a way that’s economically viable, especially as they keep talking about how premium they are?

    Before we get into this, let me make sure we’re all on the same page when it comes to terms. This post isn’t about the premium cabin on domestic flights, which is often referred to as first class. Instead, it’s about international flights that have a cabin above business class, when it’s marketed as first class. So this would include airlines on my list of the world’s best first class products.

    Airline executives are divided on the merits of having an international first class cabin. Some insist that there’s no need for such a cabin, as business class has improved so much. Meanwhile others absolutely see merit to such a product.

    I mean, just look at how carriers like Air France, Lufthansa, Singapore Airlines, and SWISS, are all investing in first class. I think Air France’s La Premiere first class is the perfect example of the upside such a product has for an airline:.

So how is it that carriers like Air France, Lufthansa, SWISS, etc., can make money offering first class to the United States (primarily targeting Americans), but US airlines seemingly can’t?

    According to recent reports, the US has way too many people with tens or hundreds of millions of dollars, or even billions of dollars. There are plenty of people who would pay to fly private, and would pay for Air France La Premiere first class, but would never consider paying the high price for first class on a US carrier, because it’s just not worth it.

    When they fly first class, they want this….

    It’s no surprise that first class at US carriers has historically failed. In many ways, it reflects the failures of the industry from decades past. In other words, first class has long been thought of as “upgrade class,” rather than something actually worth paying for. US carriers have managed to change that narrative on domestic flights, but not so much on international flights.

    According to recent reports, call it a hot take, but I think international first class absolutely could succeed at a US carrier, if done right, with a couple of caveats. Let me start with the two main hurdles that would need to be overcome, and I’ll acknowledge, this might just be the biggest problem:.

    If those hurdles could be overcome, here’s the play, as I see it (and yes, this is largely inspired by Air France La Premiere):.

    In a recent development, I think the halo effect of something like this would be massive as well. Seriously, US airline executives love to talk about how premium they are, but they can’t even introduce a top-end product, despite having access to the most lucrative customer base in the world.

    It has been revealed that in terms of economics, let me also point out that the opportunity cost of a first class cabin isn’t actually that high. “Premium” is all the rage, so what you do here is eliminate some economy seats:.

    At this point, no airline from the United States offers first class on international flights anymore. For airlines that can’t stop talking about how unbelievably premium they are, I find that to be a pretty perplexing reality. I know that many people have just accepted “oh, a good business class is the future,” but I have a different take.

    I think no US carrier actually being able to offer a globally competitive product is a failure in strategy and creativity. They have access to the world’s most lucrative customer base, and other airlines can seemingly make money serving US customers with a first class product. The problem is, US carriers have long not actually given people a reason to fly first class, all while offering too much capacity.

    Personally I think there would be a lot of merit to an international first class product that’s boutique, and is operated in the right markets. That’s not to say that I think it’ll happen — I don’t — but I do think it could succeed. The only real hurdle to overcome would be how to ensure good service….

    • Recent findings suggest that southwest and French Bee are joining forces to expand international travel options for passengers not only on both sides of the Atlantic, but also the Pacific.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that southwest and French Bee are joining forces to expand international travel options for passengers not only on both sides of the Atlantic, but also the Pacific. The two carriers announced a latest interline partnership that will allow travelers to combine flights on both airlines under a single ticket.

    Industry observers note that the agreement connects French Bee’s international network with Southwest’s extensive domestic network in the U.S. The partnership will provide connections through French Bee’s three U.S. gateway airports that Southwest also serves: Los Angeles, Miami, and San Francisco.

    French Bee also flies to Newark, New Jersey, but Southwest does not offer service there.

    Passengers will be able to connect between French Bee’s international flights and Southwest domestic flights without having to purchase separate tickets for each airline or recheck bags at each airline.

    French Bee operates an all-Airbus A350 fleet, with its primary hub located at Paris-Orly Airport, and operations to North America and destinations in the Indian Ocean and South Pacific.

    Sources indicate that southwest passengers will gain access to French Bee destinations not only from Paris, but also Tahiti in French Polynesia, which the French carrier flies to from San Francisco. The partnership will also offer one-stop French Bee connections from Paris to the Maldives and Sri Lanka, scheduled to launch in December 2026, along with current flights to Reunion Island.

    In a recent development, for French Bee customers, the new arrangement provides access to a much larger network of domestic destinations throughout the U.S. Southwest’s network includes cities such as Las Vegas, Chicago, Dallas, Denver, Nashville, Austin, San Diego, Phoenix, and multiple destinations in the Hawaiian Islands.

    The agreement represents another step in Southwest’s expanding international connectivity strategy, as the airline continues to develop relationships with overseas carriers rather than rely exclusively on its own international operations with its all-Boeing 737 fleet.

    Tickets for connecting flights are now available through French Bee’s website.

    • Some Senate Democrats have heartburn about President Donald Trump’s planned Thursday meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, but Republicans counter by saying he could get the Russian and Chinese leaders to budge on a list of problems even as he appears politically weakened at home.
    • Industry observers note that trump arrived Wednesday in China’s Shenzhen economic zone on the banks of the Pearl River ahead of a high-level summit that was ostensibly slated to focus on paring each countries’ nuclear arsenal.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that president Donald Trump prepares to shake hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China's President Xi Jinping looks on before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. (Iori Sagisawa / POOL / AFP via Getty Images).

    Some Senate Democrats have heartburn about President Donald Trump’s planned Thursday meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, but Republicans counter by saying he could get the Russian and Chinese leaders to budge on a list of problems even as he appears politically weakened at home.

    Industry observers note that trump arrived Wednesday in China’s Shenzhen economic zone on the banks of the Pearl River ahead of a high-level summit that was ostensibly slated to focus on paring each countries’ nuclear arsenal. But before he left, Trump signaled the three-way talks also likely would include the artificial intelligence race, Moscow’s bloody war with Ukraine, global trade and his standoff with Iran.

    It has been revealed that the U.S. commander in chief’s tendency to sound deferential to Putin and habit of referring to Xi as a personal “friend” concerns many congressional Democrats. But Trump’s GOP allies on Capitol Hill, despite this month’s midterm election losses, still describe him as a dealmaker who has a chance to use his final years to bend Putin and Xi toward U.S. interests.

    Rick Scott, a Florida Republican who sits on the Senate Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, stated Tuesday he was hopeful that Trump could make some progress on at least one issue with the Russian and Chinese leaders.

    Recent findings suggest that “As we all know, China and Russia want to destroy our way of life,” he mentioned. “But it would be great to reduce … nuclear stockpiles and make sure we're not going to ever get attacked.

    Still, Scott sounded skeptical about two world leaders Trump has tried to keep close during his two terms. “But do I trust Xi or Putin? No, they're a bunch of liars.” Asked if he worries Trump might trust them too much, Scott replied: “I don't think he trusts him any more than I do. … I'm glad the president's trying. Hope springs eternal. But do I actually really believe something good's going to come out of it? I don't.”.

    Outgoing House Armed Services Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., stated part of Trump’s talks on Thursday “should be to make sure the world is a safer place, to make sure we don't have aggressive behavior like Russia in an unprovoked attack against Ukraine.

    “They ought to be talking about how they don't do those sorts of things, how they don't threaten their neighbors, how they don't try to intimidate through the assertion of force that they ought to be able to work together to make sure we assure a safe globe,” noted Wittman, who lost his reelection race earlier this month.

    That comment came one day after Trump told reporters as he left the White House for Asia that he sees Putin “backing down a little bit” in his conduct of the war with Ukraine.

    Industry observers note that “I think he could be tougher. I think he could be a lot tougher, frankly,” Trump remarked Monday. “I think he's backing down.”.

    Those kinds of deferential remarks about the Russian leader are a massive reason why some Democrats have heartburn about Thursday’s meeting.

    According to recent reports, senate Armed Services member Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said Tuesday that she’s concerned about the Shenzhen summit because “I’m not sure what’s going to pop out of [Trump’s] mouth next — especially for a meeting with two guys he clearly likes.”.

    Sources indicate that sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., also a member of the Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, mentioned he has “high hopes” for the trilateral meeting — but “maybe not high expectations.”.

    According to recent reports, “I have some points of anxiety. I'm nervous about any discussion about Ukraine that doesn't involve the Ukrainians. And, so, some of the advance to this is like, ‘We're going to talk about ending the Ukraine war.’ You can't do that without Ukraine at the table,” Kaine said. “So the desire to bring about more peace and stability, that's a good thing to talk about. But no conditions about Ukraine and ending that war without them at the table? Not so sure about that.”.

    It has been revealed that during remarks Tuesday on the Senate floor, Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer criticized what he described as Trump’s misplaced priorities.

    Industry observers note that “Enforcement of the new rules restricting China’s access to our most sensitive AI chips should start today,” the New York Democrat remarked, adding that Trump should focus more of his Asia swing on securing commitments from U.S. allies to block China from gaining an upper hand in the AI technology race.

    Trump touted just that on Tuesday during remarks in Manila at a U.S.-Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in the Philippines.

    “Since I returned to office, we've made major trade deals with Malaysia, Cambodia, Indonesia, as well as Japan, South Korea, and almost everybody, frankly, at the table,” he remarked. “And we've made many other vital agreements across the region spanning energy, critical minerals and technology.”.

    But on Wednesday, Trump appeared to have pivoted to the trip’s main event.

    According to recent reports, he stood beside Xi at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen and smiled as Putin approached. Trump extended his hand and shook Putin’s as the Chinese leader looked on.

    Scott, a Trump ally in the Senate, noted Tuesday he sees the president “trying to build relationships to try to make sure we don't end up at war [because] he doesn't like war.”.

    It has been revealed that trump signaled Monday that he might press Xi for details on an alleged Chinese spy who had an affair with Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, costing the AI mogul his job as the manufacturer’s president and CEO. He also mentioned he could bring up Nvidia’s sales of sophisticated microchips that many lawmakers — Republican and Democrat — want to ensure remain in the U.S. for domestic AI development.

    According to recent reports, the administration’s response to the turmoil at Nvidia, with Trump even suggesting he'd support Huang returning as CEO, is a rare area where Republicans have expressed concern publicly. House Energy and Commerce Committee Chair Brett Guthrie, R-Kent., wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Wednesday seeking information about “the implementation of federal laws governing technology exports, in particular the application of export controls relating to semiconductor chips, the effect of which has a broad impact on America’s race with China to artificial intelligence (AI) dominance and the ability of U.S. companies to set global technology standards.”.

    Heather Williams, director of the Project on Nuclear Issues at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, wrote this week that for the three leaders, the “path is fraught with challenges.”.

    According to recent reports, “Putin could diplomatically outmaneuver the Trump administration and make any progress on nuclear concerns dependent on undermining Western support to Ukraine,” she wrote in an analysis for the Washington, D.C.-based think tank. “Even the optics of Trump and Putin negotiating while the war continues and as Russia ramps up missile strikes on Ukrainian civilian targets could be interpreted as undermining U.S. values.”.

    #122693. Industry News: Here’s Why The Boeing 777X Won’t Let Pilots Take Off With Its Wings Still Folded

    Industry News: Here’s Why The Boeing 777X Won’t Let Pilots Take Off With Its Wings Still Folded

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1516 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that the Boeing 777X cannot take off with its wingtips folded due to critical safety and aerodynamic reasons.
    • While the 777X is physically capable of remaining airborne with its wingtips folded, it is strictly prohibited and operationally restricted from doing so by both design and regulation.
    • The 777X uses a revolutionary wingtip folding system designed and manufactured by Liebherr-Aerospace at its center of excellence in Lindenberg, Germany.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that the Boeing 777X cannot take off with its wingtips folded due to critical safety and aerodynamic reasons. The extended wingtips are essential for the 777X's designed lift and fuel efficiency. Taking off with them folded would significantly increase drag and reduce lift, potentially compromising the aircraft's safety during the critical takeoff phase.

    While the 777X is physically capable of remaining airborne with its wingtips folded, it is strictly prohibited and operationally restricted from doing so by both design and regulation. The aircraft is equipped with escalating warning systems that alert pilots if the wingtips are not extended and locked before entering a runway. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) certification requires these systems to effectively prevent the aircraft from taking off in a folded configuration.

    The 777X uses a revolutionary wingtip folding system designed and manufactured by Liebherr-Aerospace at its center of excellence in Lindenberg, Germany. This system is a first for commercial aviation and allows the aircraft to maintain high-efficiency aerodynamics in flight while fitting into standard airport gates designed for smaller aircraft.

    The 3.5-meter (approx. 11 feet) wingtips are operated by a complex actuation system that transitions them between folded (vertical) and extended (horizontal) positions. The movement is driven by a hydraulic power drive unit (PDU) and geared rotary actuators. The full transition takes approximately 20 seconds.

    Recent findings suggest that once extended, the wingtips are secured by latch-pin and secondary-lock actuators. During flight, the mechanism is mechanically locked with a large bolt and electronically isolated. This ensures the wingtips cannot move even if there is a power failure.

    It has been revealed that A wider wingspan moves the wingtip vortices further away from the fuselage. This reduces the downwash on the wing, allowing it to generate more lift with less drag. The larger surface area creates more lift, reducing the thrust required from the GE9X engines to stay airborne. This results in a roughly 10%-12% improvement in fuel efficiency compared to previous generations and competitors.

    The 777X integrates advanced aerodynamics with digital flight controls to deliver a ride that is significantly more efficient and comfortable than its predecessors. The extra span enables the 777X to climb faster and cruise at higher, more efficient altitudes where air resistance is lower.

    Made from carbon-fiber reinforced plastic, these wings are thinner and lighter than traditional aluminum wings. This allows for the massive span without a prohibitive weight penalty. With GE9X engines, these aerodynamics result in lower fuel burn than competing aircraft like the Airbus A350, and a 20% lower fuel consumption rate than the legacy 747, which it is designed to replace.

    Industry observers note that the 777X features Smooth Ride Technology, an advanced fly-by-wire system adapted from the 787 Dreamliner, designed to neutralize turbulence actively. Hundreds of sensors detect air disturbances in real-time. The flight computer then automatically actuates the control surfaces, specifically the flaperons, to damp vertical motion and pitch that passengers feel during turbulence.

    In a recent development, the highly flexible composite wings act like giant shock absorbers, bending and flexing during flight to absorb gust loads rather than transmitting those forces directly to the cabin. Beyond the ride quality,the 777X offers a lower cabin altitude (6,000 feet) and higher humidity. These environmental improvements, combined with 40% less engine noise, help reduce jet lag and physical fatigue on long-haul flights.

    In a recent development, the folding mechanism is not designed to handle the massive aerodynamic loads encountered during takeoff and flight while in the "up" position. Attempting a flight with them folded could lead to mechanical failure or the tips breaking off.

    It has been revealed that boeing integrated multiple fail-safes into the flight systems to prevent such an occurrence. If the wingtips are not extended and locked, the aircraft's takeoff warning system (required by the FAA and EASA) will trigger a loud alarm when the pilot adds power.

    In a recent development, boeing implemented an electronic checklist that confirms the position of the wingtips. If the flight crew attempts to initiate a takeoff procedure, the system will indicate “incomplete” until the wingtips are extended. If the pilots begin to take off roll without extending the wingtips, the avionics in the 777x will no longer trigger an aborted takeoff once the plane reaches 50 knots ground speed.

    Interestingly, Boeing had already explored folding wingtips for the original 777 in the mid-1990s, even patenting a design. However, that version was heavy and complex; the technology only became commercially viable with the advancements in materials and actuation seen in the 777X. Combining advances in newly introduced material science with the newly acquired archives of McDonnell Douglas made it a natural evolution to develop the next-generation Boeing widebody with folding wings.

    According to recent reports, in its 1997 merger with McDonnell Douglas, Boeing inherited the F/A-18 Super Hornet program. The pivotal deal that integrated decades of naval aviation expertise into Boeing’s defense portfolio. By combining with the storied warplane manufacturer, Boeing inherited a rich legacy of naval fighter jet engineering and design. Looking past the hornet, the annals of the McDonnell portfolio include the most mass-produced supersonic naval fighter ever made, the F-4 Phantom II.

    Sources indicate that in naval aviation, wing folding is often a manual pilot action verified by ground crews. For the 777X, Boeing automated the process to reduce pilot workload: the wingtips automatically fold when ground speed drops below 50 knots after landing. Unlike the Super Hornet, where a significant portion of the wing folds, the 777X only folds the outer 3.5 meters (11 feet) of its tip. This minimizes the weight penalty and places the hinge where structural loads are lower compared to a mid-wing fold.

    Industry observers note that the 777X incorporates "spill-over" benefits from military R&D, specifically in the use of high-redundancy sensors and fail-safe locking pins that ensure the wing is structurally one piece before the engines can reach takeoff power. Boeing had to prove to the FAA that its upcoming commercial mechanism could withstand aerodynamic loads equivalent to a fixed wing, leveraging testing methodologies honed over decades of military carrier operations.

    Sources indicate that in 1995, Boeing patented a design for folding wingtips on the original 777, but the proposal was abandoned because airlines rejected the idea. The primary reasons for its abandonment were the added weight, reduced fuel capacity, and increased maintenance costs associated with the design.

    The main objective was to allow the widebody aircraft to fit into existing "Code E" airport gates, as initial designs anticipated a wingspan that might exceed standard limits. The original proposal featured a hinge positioned closer to the wing root, with the outer 21 feet (6.4 meters) of each wing designed to fold upward.

    Sources indicate that airlines found the engineering solution overly complex. The hinge's location negatively affected fuel capacity and added significant structural weight, making the trade-offs in performance and cost unacceptable at the time. The concept was not entirely discarded and was later refined and implemented in the current Boeing 777X program, which features a much larger, more fuel-efficient carbon-fiber composite wing.

    The folding mechanism on the 777X is placed further out on the wing, which minimizes the impact on fuel capacity and adds less weight than the 1995 design. The 777X's wingspan is significantly larger than the original 777 and would fall into the restrictive ICAO Code F category without the folding tips.

    It has been revealed that the 777X's 11-foot (3.36 meters) folding wingtips reduce the wingspan to within Code E limits when on the ground, allowing it to use most existing airport gates. This makes the aircraft more versatile and avoids costly airport infrastructure upgrades that competitors like the Airbus A380 require.

    The 777X program is famously delayed by nearly a decade. Originally slated to debut in 2020 for launch customer Lufthansa, the enormous twinjet is not expected to enter full-rate production until 2027. Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg stated this year that the organization has “a mountain of work” ahead of it for certification. These delays are in no small part due to the 737 MAX disasters, with two fatal crashes in 2018 and 2019 that caused the death of 350 Souls.

    In a recent development, as the legendary American planemaker has course-corrected in the years following the tragic mishaps of the latest and greatest iteration of the 737, narrowbody mainline airliner, the 777X program has faced additional headwinds. The company refocused on quality control and pushed ahead to ensure that all airframes remain as high-quality as they have always been, since the days when passengers would say, "if it's not Boeing, I'm not going.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the Dubai Airshow 2025 reaffirmed customer confidence in the 777X, as the colossal twinjet offers the only viable replacement for the world's aging fleets of jumbo jets, such as the Airbus A380 and the legacy Boeing 747. Emirates, which is the world's leading widebody operator, upped its order for 65 more of the forthcoming 777X. The aircraft promises to usher in a newly introduced era of commercial aviation, which we look forward to witnessing when the day comes.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I just got back to Rio after a quick trip to Ireland for Aer Lingus’ event to showcase their new A330 cabins, including its first-ever premium economy.

    I flew Air France economy both ways, and I’m glad I resisted the offer of $420 during online check-in to upgrade the outbound overnight economy leg. Ironically, it was the long day-flight back where I actually wished I’d upgraded.

    Industry observers note that however, to answer the economy vs. premium economy question, it all comes down to maximising comfort, and I think this is easier to do in economy than premium economy.

    If, like me, sleeping upright or on your back is almost impossible, then what follows will likely apply to you.

    The main reason I’m deterred to pick premium economy for overnight flights is because of the fixed armrests, where tray tables are sometimes stowed in this cabin.

    Despite the extra recline and leg rest element (which sometimes makes it even harder to get comfortable), the fixed armrests restrict the ability to sleep any way other than straight like a pencil.

    To make matters worse, they stop you from lying across more than one seat if you find yourself in an empty row.

    According to recent reports, it’s for that reason that I much prefer economy. While having a row to yourself isn’t guaranteed, there’s at least a chance of being able to move around the cabin, or stretch out into an empty seat. No matter where you sit or how empty the cabin is, you can’t do that in premium economy.

    Another element of my pre-trip planning that I expect many of you to relate to is the fact it takes me so long umming and aahing over the best seat to pick.

    Thanks to my Flying Blue Gold status (SkyTeam Elite Plus), I could pick any seat in the economy cabin of the Boeing 777-200ER for free from 72 hours before departure.

    According to recent reports, I narrowed it down to an empty seat in the exit row, and the only row of three with an empty middle seat. I didn’t even consider one of the many empty middle rows of four seats in case they filled up before take off and I ended up in an aisle with no window to rest my head. Using the window or plane’s fuselage to rest my head on is the only saving grace for me when trying to sleep sitting upright.

    As the empty exit seat would have the same restricting fixed partition as premium, I decided against that, too.

    After the “boarding complete” announcement was made, the middle seat in my row remained empty, and there were three seats free in the middle of row 25, a row in front. I explained to the girl in the aisle seat that if one of us moved to the other row, we’d both have three seats to ourselves. She didn’t seem to understand my point, and said she’d prefer to sit in the aisle than us both have three free seats to ourselves.

    I didn’t want to move to the middle seats either, so I got as comfortable as I could using the middle seat and the pillow I brought from home.

    It has been revealed that in the end, I did manage to get some half decent curled up shut eye (the thick pillow protected my back from the hard parts of the seat when propped against the fuselage). However, when I went to the loo, I noticed some people in the rear cabin had got lucky and were fast asleep spread across a whole four seats.

    Maybe I’ll take more of a risk next time….

    I’m not saying economy is always a better choice than premium. For example, I’d always recommend Emirates’ pretty darn impressive premium economy over economy, because it genuinely is several steps up from economy.

    Sources indicate that if it was up to me, I’d have had a lie-flat seat for the overnight segment. I didn’t, and I’m pretty certain I got better sleep quality curled up across two seats in economy that I would have almost upright on my back in premium.

    Would you ever choose economy over premium economy?

    #122690. How to Spend 3 Perfect Days in Naples

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1602 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    How to Spend 3 Perfect Days in Naples

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1602 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A fascinating, complex, and multi-layered city, Naples is brimming with contradictions.
    • Industry observers note that I’ve been visiting for over 30 years and have seen huge changes, most of them positive.
    • You could easily spend two weeks in Naples and not see everything.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A fascinating, complex, and multi-layered city, Naples is brimming with contradictions. Dilapidated, neglected neighborhoods share city space with splendid palaces and world-beating museums. The city’s origins go back to the ancient Greeks, yet the contemporary art scene here is buzzing. There is a state-of-the-art metro system designed by renowned artists and architects (no wonder, since the traffic is infamously heavy).

    Industry observers note that I’ve been visiting for over 30 years and have seen huge changes, most of them positive. Naples today is safer, more tourist-friendly, and cleaner than ever before, yet it remains Italy’s most beguiling city. The eating and drinking scene has evolved, there is a much wider choice of places to stay (with Rocco Forte due to open a hotel here in 2027), and museums and monuments have been spruced up and reorganized. In 2027, the America’s Cup will arrive as well.

    You could easily spend two weeks in Naples and not see everything. But if you only have three days, start early and be prepared to pack in as much as possible; you can rest once you get home. Here is my advice for how to make the most of it.

    You coudl easily spend two weeks in Naples and not see everything—but three days are a delicious taste, too.

    In a recent development, historic Gran Caffè Gambrinus is a perfect place to start your first day, shoulder to shoulder with the locals at the bar for a shot of espresso and a warm cornetto (only tourists sit on the terrace). Just across Piazza Trieste e Trento lies the imposing dark grey and red Palazzo Reale where you can visit the sumptuous Royal Apartments and ornate Teatrino, and on the other side is the Teatro San Carlo, one of Italy’s most prestigious opera houses; opera buffs can book a behind-the-scenes tour, or even better, tickets for a performance.

    It has been revealed that from the Toledo metro station, you get full immersion in the Stazione d’Arte, a public art project involving some of the greatest contemporary artists and architects who have transformed Naples’ main underground stations into public galleries. Dominated by Oscar Tusquets Blanca’s jaw-dropping mosaic, Toledo is one of the most impressive—but for just the price of a metro ticket (just over $2), you can tour them all.

    A quick walk north on Via Toledo leads to Via della Pignasecca, where you can catch the end of the lively morning market with its troughs of slithering, glistening fish and seafood, piles of seasonal fruit and vegetables, and stalls selling everything from tripe to knock-off designer handbags.

    Lunch at no-nonsense Trattoria da Nenella near Piazza Carità is a noisy, fun experience; you’ll probably have to queue, but the deep-fried anchovies and meatballs in tomato sauce are worth it, and prices are rock-bottom.

    The Cappella Sansevero is home to Giuseppe Sammartino’s sublime 1753 marble Cristo Velato.

    It has been revealed that after a shot of the best coffee in the city at Café Mexico in Piazza Dante, you can spend the afternoon exploring the grid of streets around the so-called Spaccanapoli, the heart of Roman Neapolis where ancient monuments rub shoulders with street food stalls, tiny grocers, once-grand palazzi, and shops selling tourist trinkets and religious memorabilia. Piazza del Gesù, at the western end, is dominated by the eponymous church and an ornate roccoco ‘guglia’. Just to the east is the Church and Convent of Santa Chiara with a beautiful Gothic interior and a cloister famous for its bright, 18th-century majolica tiles. Close by is Naples’ most celebrated (and most crowded) sight, the Cappella Sansevero, home to Giuseppe Sammartino’s sublime 1753 marble Cristo Velato.

    Sources indicate that back on the Spaccanapoli, nip into Gay-Odin (n. 61) for a chocolate gelato and then continue to the vast Duomo where you will be dazzled by the gilt-encrusted Cappella di San Gennaro and the subterranean church of Santa Restituita and its 4th-century baptistery.

    Recent findings suggest that close by are the chapel of Pio Monte della Misericordia with Caravaggio’s seminal Seven Acts of Mercy and crumbling Piazza San Girolamini where Banksy’s Madonna with a Pistol appeared on the back right-hand wall in 2004. San Lorenzo Maggiore is an essential visit if you want to understand multi-layered Naples; under the 13th-century church, ongoing excavations have revealed the astonishing remains of a Greco-Roman city dating back 2,000 years.

    In a recent development, A detour down Via San Gregorio Armeno takes you past shops selling pastori or figurines for Christmas cribs. Much of what you see is mass-produced these days, so for the real deal, visit Marco Ferrigno’s workshop at number 10. Continue to leafy Piazza Bellini, a lively evening hub, and bag a terrace table at Café Intramoenia for a Campari spritz—you’ve earned it.

    For dinner, Europeo di Mattozzi is a personal favorite for its echoes of elegant old Naples; the classic food is fantastic (try the sublime melanzane alla parmigiana and the pasta with potatoes and provola cheese), the host Alfonso is charming, and your fellow diners are likely to be mostly locals.

    Use Castel dell'Ovoa as your launchpad for a classic Neapolitan passeggiata along the wide, traffic-free seafront drag.

    Recent findings suggest that day two starts where it all began. Parthenope—later Neapolis and later still Napoli—was founded more than 2,500 years ago on the tiny island of Megaris, now occupied by the Castel dell’Ovo and the picturesque fishing hamlet of Borgo Marinari. There’s nothing much to see in the castle, but it’s a good launch pad for the classic Neapolitan passeggiata along the wide, traffic-free seafront drag. It’s lined with restaurants and cafés offering tables in the sun for a cappuccino and magnificent views.

    It has been revealed that the delightful neighbourhood of Chiaia is a criss-cross of pretty cobbled lanes peppered with independent boutiques, cool bars, and tiny restaurants; Via dei Mille and Via dei Filangeri are known for designer clothes and chic galleries. The handmade silk ties at tiny, old-fashioned Marinella make wonderful gifts, and a counter perch at tiny Pescheria Mattiucci is a good choice for a quick seafood lunch with a glass of something chilled and white.

    Depending on the weather (and energy levels), one option from here is to head west beyond Mergellina to the upmarket seaside suburb of Posillipo for an afternoon on the beach; sunbeds and umbrellas can be rented at Bagno Sirena.

    Or you can hop on the Funicolare di Chiaia and trundle up to leafy Vomero and the panoramic Certosa di San Martino, a Carthusian monastery complex with an ornate church, several museums, two cloisters, and the famous Monk’s Cemetery decorated with marble skulls. It also has knock-out views over the whole waterfront and the Bay of Naples to the Sorrentine Peninsula. The Friggitoria Vomero—one of the city’s few remaining authentic ‘frying shops’—doles out sizzling snacks from 6 p.m. and is conveniently close to the funicolare stop as you head back down the hill.

    Chiaia’s quiet lanes morph into a nightlife hub from aperitivo hour on, filling up with smartly dressed locals and visitors in search of a good night out. Cocktail spot per eccellenza is retro-glam Antiquario where the jacketed barmen mix a stonking Negroni. From here it’s a short stroll to tiny Ristorante Dora, open since 1973, for textbook versions of fish and seafood classics such as spaghetti alle vongole (with local clams). Head back to Chiaia for a nightcap; follow your nose and the party crowd.

    The atmospheric burial site of Cimitero delle Fontanelle is a respite from the buzzing streets above.

    A no-go area for tourists until relatively recently, the dilapidated, densely populated but intriguing Rione Sanità is Naples in the raw. Breakfast at Pasticceria Popella in Via Arena alla Sanità is a must for their sfogliatelle and cream-stuffed ‘fiocchi di neve’ before having a rummage among the market stalls and tiny shops on Via dei Vergini; at n. 19 is the grand entrance to the famous pale green and cream Palazzo dello Spagnuolo with its celebrated ‘flying staircase’ by local architect Ferdinando San Felice.

    These shambolic streets are filled with tooting cars, buzzing vespas, and bewildered tourists, but there are hidden artistic gems too: the 2,400 year-old recently restored Ipogeo dei Cristallini, the atmospheric burial site of the Cimitero delle Fontanelle with its piles of skulls and bones; and the labyrinthine Catacombs of San Gaudioso under the basilica of Santa Maria della Sanità.

    You can’t visit the Sanità without a meal at Ciro Oliva’s crazy-lively temple to pizza Concettina ai Tre Santi (booking is essential), where the tasting menus offer an endless succession of slices topped with whatever the pizzaiolo dreams up at the time.

    Naples’ Archaeological Museum (aka Mann) houses one of the world’s great collections of ancient art and artefacts, and if you only visit one museum, make it this. Must-sees include the monumental Roman sculptures on the ground floor, the collection of ancient erotica in the Gabinetto Segreto, and the dazzling mosaics, wall paintings, and bronzes from Pompeii and Herculaneum.

    Afterwards, check out the brilliant selection of exquisite handmade gloves at factory prices in the workshops of Omega, a family glove business that first opened in 1923, before winding up the day in the surprisingly peaceful oasis of the exotic Orto Botanico gardens on traffic-clogged Via Foria.

    For a last blast, Grand Hotel Parker’s on the way up to Vomero is the smart place to go. Cocktails and light bites are served on the rooftop terrace while on the floor below, chef Domenico Candela whips up a storm with his two-Michelin-star take on local cuisine to a backdrop of unforgettable views.

    #122689. Industry News: Third Time’s Not The Charm: A SWISS A220’s Odd Triple Aborted Takeoff

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (985 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Onemileatatime ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Third Time’s Not The Charm: A SWISS A220’s Odd Triple Aborted Takeoff

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (985 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If you’re a frequent flyer, odds are that you’ve encountered an aborted takeoff, whereby the plane accelerates down the runway, only to slow down, and eventually come to a stop.
    • In a recent development, however, here’s something you don’t often see — a SWISS Airbus A220 aborted its takeoff three times in a row, before finally returning to the gate to see what was going on, as reported by Blick.
    • It has been revealed that on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, SWISS flight LX2110 was scheduled to operate from Zurich (ZRH) to Malaga (AGP), with a 9:35AM departure.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If you’re a frequent flyer, odds are that you’ve encountered an aborted takeoff, whereby the plane accelerates down the runway, only to slow down, and eventually come to a stop. In some cases this can feel like a non-event, while in other cases it can feel much scarier, depending on the speed at which the takeoff is aborted.

    In a recent development, however, here’s something you don’t often see — a SWISS Airbus A220 aborted its takeoff three times in a row, before finally returning to the gate to see what was going on, as reported by Blick. The explanation is actually quite logical, but that doesn’t make the whole ordeal any less unusual.

    It has been revealed that on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, SWISS flight LX2110 was scheduled to operate from Zurich (ZRH) to Malaga (AGP), with a 9:35AM departure. The flight was operated by an Airbus A220-300 with the registration code HB-JCM.

    Sources indicate that the plane pushed back and taxied out to the runway right on schedule. The pilots began the takeoff roll, but then rapidly applied the brakes, causing the plane to come to a stop, while still at a slow speed. The pilots took a moment to run checklists, and then decided on another takeoff attempt, only for the same thing to happen again!

    Sources indicate that after the second aborted takeoff, the captain reportedly informed passengers that the thrust levers had popped out during the takeoff roll, and that was the reason for the aborted takeoff. However, rather than returning to the gate, they decided to attempt an additional takeoff roll.

    Once again, the takeoff was aborted. At that point the captain explained that nothing like this had ever happened to him before in his 12 year career, and that the plane would be returning to the gate.

    There ended up being a plane change, and then the A220 with the registration code HB-JCO was assigned to operate this flight — it ended up taking off at 1:29PM and landing at 3:52PM, around 3.5 hours behind schedule.

    A SWISS spokesperson confirmed the incident happened, though noted that the takeoffs were aborted at a low speed of around 50 kilometers per hour (around 30 miles per hour).

    Recent findings suggest that what explains the aborted takeoffs? Well, it was because as the plane accelerated for takeoff, the automatic thrust control system automatically deactivated. To explain this as simply as possible, as I understand it, on the A220 when the auto-thrust is armed and the thrust levers are moved forward for takeoff, the auto-thrust then takes over, and moves the levers forward without manual intervention.

    Industry observers note that in other words, one of the pilots keeps their hands on the auto-thrust levers and “moves” with them, but doesn’t actually apply any force. Pilots are trained this way, and to not manually apply force. In the event that the crew tries to stop the auto-thrust lever motion, a pressure switch detects this, and then disengages the auto-thrust, to allow for a manual override.

    Industry observers note that in this case, the auto-thrust incorrectly detected resistance, when the pilots weren’t attempting to apply it. According to the airline, the system that monitors the aircraft’s technical status in real time was unable to identify the cause of the error, as no errors were displayed in the system. So at first, the pilots likely wondered if they had accidentally applied force.

    However, once technicians had a look at the plane, it was discovered that the switch for disabling the automatic thrust control on the original aircraft was stuck, and this caused the automatic thrust control to shut down during takeoff attempts.

    So while this can understandably seem scary to passengers, this wasn’t even a direct safety issue. After all, the pilots could’ve also manually moved the throttles. However, you also don’t want to take off when you know there’s an issue with the throttles, since that’s not exactly a best practice.

    A SWISS Airbus A220 attempted a takeoff from Zurich three times in a row. While I’ve had two consecutive aborted takeoffs, I’ve never had three, and I can’t imagine that happens all too often.

    Industry observers note that while this is unusual, it sounds like this was handled well, and I can see why the pilots kept trying. This wasn’t a critical safety glitch, but instead, just an incorrect detection of inputs, in a way that wouldn’t really pose a risk to the flight. At the same time, you don’t want to knowingly take off with a fault switch.

    What do you make of this SWISS aborted takeoff trio?

    #122686. FCC pick advanced by Senate Commerce after Democratic boycott

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (888 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    FCC pick advanced by Senate Commerce after Democratic boycott

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (888 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ted Cruz, R-Texas, talks with reporters after the Senate luncheons in the Capitol on Tuesday.
    • The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.
    • Republicans on the Commerce Committee voted unanimously to advance the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, to be a member of the commission, alongside several transportation and communications bills.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, talks with reporters after the Senate luncheons in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.

    Republicans on the Commerce Committee voted unanimously to advance the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, to be a member of the commission, alongside several transportation and communications bills.

    The fate of the nominations and bills could ultimately be decided via a challenge on the Senate floor, according to a Democratic committee staffer, speaking on condition of anonymity.

    In a statement Wednesday morning, committee Democrats, led by ranking member  Maria Cantwell of Washington, noted they objected to Thumann Severs’ nomination without a Democratic “pair” nomination and referenced a letter they sent to Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, on Monday requesting the nomination be removed from the agenda.

    “Commissioner Anna Gomez could be re-nominated with all swiftness, as we have called for numerous times,” the group wrote. “This is not a problem we created, but a problem that the White House can solve.”.

    According to recent reports, thumann Severs, if confirmed, would give the FCC three Republican members and one Democrat, Gomez. The three Republicans could then constitute a quorum on the commission, allowing President Donald Trump to potentially fire Gomez. The commission generally has five members, three of the president’s party and two in the minority.

    Cruz stated at the markup that there is nothing in the law that requires moving nominees in pairs, and that committee Republicans would continue their work on what he called a nomination that followed a “typical process.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January,” Cruz said. “But today is November 18th. The American people elected each of us to fulfill our duties, including advice and consent, for our full terms.”.

    Related: Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing.

    The Democratic staffer told reporters that because the committee did not adopt rules at the beginning of the 119th Congress, it has been operating under rules from the 118th, which required the attendance of at least one member of the minority party to constitute a quorum for reporting bills or nominations.

    In a recent development, “The remaining recourse is to basically go to the floor and . . . make an inquiry in terms of what took place today, and then there would have to be a formal ruling by the chair,” they said.

    They added that in determining whether the committee had a quorum to advance the nomination, “It would depend on how they view our committee rules from the 118th that we practice under for the 119th versus what the Senate rules are.” The staffer remarked they have not yet spoken with committee Democrats or Democratic leadership about plans for such an inquiry.

    Democrats also previously boycotted a committee markup in March over an aviation safety bill left off the committee’s agenda, after which action was deferred. The committee later came to agreement and rescheduled the markup.

    In their letter Monday, Democrats quoted Cruz from a 2014 statement about the nomination of Loretta Lynch to be attorney general.

    “As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree,” the letter noted.

    On Tuesday, Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., wrote his own letter to Cruz calling for the removal of the nomination from the agenda based on grounds that Thumann Severs lied to the committee.

    “While Ms. Thumann testified she did not work ‘on any media-related complications,’ documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests demonstrate that she worked on several media related issues, including on commitments that Skydance made to pave the way for FCC approval of its merger with Paramount,” Luján wrote.

    Democrats have criticized the FCC and Carr for allowing media consolidation, including by Skydance. There has also been bipartisan criticism of Carr’s threats against broadcasters for speech he disagrees with.

    Luján told reporters Wednesday prior to the markup that he expects, under Democratic control next year, Carr and potentially Thumann Severs would be called to testify.

    “I have questions. I certainly hope that Brendan Carr will voluntarily show up to this committee when invited, and that other rules and tools do not need to be used,” Luján said, responding to a question about possibly subpoenaing Carr. “But . . . everything should be on the table.”.

    Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., said at the markup that he spoke with Thumann Severs about her role at the FCC and her “lack of engagement” as the commission has made decisions regarding broadcasters. He also said he found her testimony at last week’s nomination hearing “comforting.”.

    Sources indicate that “I have concerns with FCC action in regard to political speech, broadcasters, and she indicated in her answers . . . in a way that provided me with a level of comfort about her nomination in regard to that glitch,” Moran mentioned.

    Moran also noted he hopes to meet with Thumann Severs before her nomination is brought to the floor.
